title: Largest subtorus and smooth connected subgroups of groups of multiplicative type
statement: Let $k$ be a field [def-weil-field]. All group schemes below are affine group schemes [def-sc-group-scheme] of finite type [def-weil-finite-type-morphism] over $k$, and all subgroup schemes are closed [def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup]. Smoothness is as in [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms], and connectedness as in [def-weil-connected-scheme]; geometrically connected means connected after extension to an algebraic closure $\bar k$ of $k$. A torus is a group scheme becoming $(\mathbf G_m)^d$ over $\bar k$ for some integer $d\geq0$, where $\mathbf G_m$ is as in [def-sc-gm-ga]. A group scheme is of multiplicative type if over $\bar k$ it is isomorphic to a closed subgroup scheme of $(\mathbf G_m)^n$ for some $n\geq0$. Every torus is smooth and connected. Let $D$ be of multiplicative type. There is a largest subtorus $D^t\subseteq D$: it contains every subtorus of $D$. For every field extension $K/k$, the equality $(D^t)_K=(D_K)^t$ holds as subgroup schemes of $D_K$. Every closed subgroup scheme of a group of multiplicative type is of multiplicative type, and every smooth connected group scheme of multiplicative type is a torus. In particular every smooth connected closed subgroup scheme of a torus is a torus.

source.place: Theorem 12.9(c), printed p.232; Definition 12.14 and the following paragraph (tori; an algebraic subgroup of a torus is a torus if and only if it is smooth and connected), printed p.236; Definition 12.17 and following paragraph, printed p.236; Theorem 12.23 and Corollary 12.24, printed p.240; Notation 12.29, printed p.241.

proof.text: If $H\subseteq D$ is a closed subgroup, extend to $\bar k$ and choose a closed immersion $D_{\bar k}\hookrightarrow\mathbf G_m^n$. Its composition with $H_{\bar k}\hookrightarrow D_{\bar k}$ is a closed immersion: on coordinate rings it is the composite of two surjections, and after scalar extension these remain surjective because any lifted element still maps to its original tensor. Thus $H$ is of multiplicative type by the definition in the statement.

source.place: Theorem 12.9(c) and paragraph following Definition 12.17: closure under subgroups.

proof.text: For a torus $T$, $T_{\bar k}\simeq\mathbf G_m^d=D_{\bar k}(\mathbf Z^d)$. The geometric criteria show that this scheme is smooth and connected, including $d=0$. Smoothness descends along $\operatorname{Spec}\bar k\to\operatorname{Spec}k$ by the fpqc descent lemma; this map is affine, surjective, and flat because $\bar k$ is a nonzero vector space over $k$. The algebraic-closure criterion gives geometric connectedness of $T$, hence connectedness. The character equivalence and its scalar-extension identification give $X^*(T)\simeq\mathbf Z^d$ as abelian groups, so in particular this group is torsion-free.

source.place: Definition 12.14, p.236; Remark 12.5, p.232; Theorem 12.23, p.240; smoothness descent and algebraic-closure test as in the cited nodes.

proof.text: Let $H$ be smooth, connected and of multiplicative type. Its identity is a $k$-rational point, so the rational-point criterion implies that $H_{\bar k}$ is connected. Smoothness persists under this extension by the smooth base-change clause. Write $H_{\bar k}=D_{\bar k}(M)$ using the character equivalence. In characteristic $p>0$, connectedness says all torsion of $M$ is $p$-primary and smoothness says there is no nonzero $p$-primary torsion; in characteristic zero connectedness directly says $M$ is torsion-free. Since $M$ is finitely generated, the finite-basis lemma gives $M\simeq\mathbf Z^d$, and the group-algebra identification gives $H_{\bar k}\simeq\mathbf G_m^d$. Thus $H$ is a torus. Together with step 1 this proves the claimed special case for smooth connected subgroups of a torus.

source.place: Paragraph following Definition 12.17, p.236; Remark 12.5, p.232; Corollary 1.32, p.16; Definition 12.14, p.236.

proof.text: Put $M=X^*(D)$ and $A=M_{\mathrm{tors}}=\{m:\exists n>0,\ nm=0\}$. This subgroup is Galois-stable since $n\sigma(m)=\sigma(nm)$. The quotient $\overline M=M/A$ is finitely generated by images of generators of $M$ and is torsion-free: if $n(m+A)=0$, then $nm\in A$, so $rnm=0$ for some $r>0$, whence $m\in A$. The finite-basis lemma gives $\overline M\simeq\mathbf Z^d$. The character equivalence takes the surjection $q:M\twoheadrightarrow\overline M$ to a closed immersion $i:D_k(\overline M)\hookrightarrow D_k(M)=D$. Its source is a torus: by the scalar-extension clause, $X^*(D_k(\overline M)_{\bar k})\simeq X^*(D_k(\overline M))\simeq\overline M$ as abelian groups, and over $\bar k$ the Galois group is trivial, so the character equivalence over $\bar k$ gives $D_k(\overline M)_{\bar k}\simeq D_{\bar k}(\overline M)\simeq D_{\bar k}(\mathbf Z^d)\simeq\mathbf G_m^d$ by the group-algebra formula. Define $D^t$ to be this closed subtorus with inclusion $i$.

source.place: Corollary 12.24 and its proof, p.240; Notation 12.29, p.241.

proof.text: For any subtorus $j:T\hookrightarrow D$, its character map $j^*:M\to X^*(T)$ has torsion-free target by step 2. For $m\in A$ and $nm=0$ one has $n j^*(m)=0$, hence $j^*(m)=0$. Therefore $j^*$ factors uniquely through $q:M\to\overline M$. Full faithfulness of the character equivalence takes this factorization to $T\to D^t\xrightarrow{i}D$ equal to $j$. This says exactly that the closed subgroup $T$ is contained in $D^t$, proving maximality and uniqueness as a subgroup of $D$.

source.place: Notation 12.29, p.241: largest subtorus, using Theorem 12.23.

proof.text: For any field extension $K/k$, choose an algebraic closure $\bar K\supseteq\bar k$; the closed immersion $D_{\bar k}\hookrightarrow\mathbf G_m^n$ stays a closed immersion after extension to $\bar K$ (surjections of coordinate rings remain surjective, as in step 1), so $D_K$ is of multiplicative type and $(D_K)^t$ is defined by step 4 over $K$. The natural character identification $X^*(D_K)\simeq M$ preserves element orders, and therefore identifies its torsion subgroup with $A$ and its torsion quotient with $M/A$. By compatibility with character maps, the base change of the inclusion from step 4 has the same character map $q$ as the inclusion constructed for $D_K$. Full faithfulness over $K$ gives an isomorphism of these subgroups commuting with their inclusions into $D_K$. Consequently they are the same closed subgroup scheme: $(D^t)_K=(D_K)^t$. This applies to inseparable and transcendental extensions as well.

source.place: Notation 12.29, p.241; scalar-extension compatibility of the character construction in Section 12(g), pp.239--240.

split_report.summary: Constructed the largest torus using the torsion-free character quotient, proved maximality by explicit factorization of character maps, and verified arbitrary scalar extension. The statement is unchanged.
